title: Regularization II - Lasso Regression (L1)
abstract:
Lasso replaces Ridge's squared penalty with an absolute one, and that single
change transforms shrinkage into selection: some weights become exactly
zero, so Lasso performs feature selection as a side effect of fitting. This
document derives the soft-thresholding operator that produces the zeros, gives
the diamond-versus-circle geometry, explains the notes' memorable intuition that
$\lambda$ "feels like it is in the numerator for Lasso and the denominator for
Ridge", covers why there is no closed form and how coordinate descent solves it,
and states Lasso's real limitations with correlated features.

blocks.t: The Idea
From the notes

items:
Lasso regression reduces overfitting by shrinking weights; some
 weights become exactly zero.
Thus effectively it does feature selection.

Loss $=$ Loss $+$ Penalty — add an absolute penalty on
 the coefficients.

blocks.t: \boxed{ L=\text{Loss}+\lambda\left|m\right| },\qquad \lambda\ge0

items: Higher lambda $\to$ underfit.
Lower lambda $\to$ overfitting.

blocks.t: Written out

The only difference from Ridge is $|\beta_j|$ in place of $\beta_j^2$. As with
Ridge, the intercept is not penalised.

blocks.cap:
Coefficient paths for the same data under both penalties. Ridge's
 coefficients decay smoothly and asymptotically. Lasso's hit exactly zero at
 finite $\lambda$ and stay there — the visual signature of selection.

blocks.t: Why Lasso Creates Sparsity
From the notes

As $\lambda$ increases, the corresponding coefficients become zero. For
Ridge they get near to 0; for Lasso exactly 0.

It feels like $\lambda$ is in the numerator in Lasso and in the denominator
in Ridge.
Why that intuition is literally correct
In the orthonormal case ($X^{\!\top}X=I$) both problems have closed forms:
where $(z)_+ = \max(z,0)$. This is the soft-thresholding operator.

Division by $1+\lambda$ shrinks proportionally and can never reach zero.
Subtracting $\lambda/2$ and clipping at zero sets every coefficient
smaller than $\lambda/2$ to exactly zero. That is the whole mechanism.

blocks.cap:
Left: the number of non-zero coefficients. Ridge keeps all twelve at
 every $\lambda$; Lasso prunes down towards the four that are genuinely
 non-zero. Right: the two shrinkage operators. Lasso's has a flat region around
 the origin — the dead zone that produces the zeros.

blocks.t: The derivation of soft-thresholding
Where the kink comes from
For a single coefficient with $X^{\!\top}X=I$, minimise

g(\beta)=(\beta-b)^{2}+\lambda|\beta|,
 \qquad b=\hat\beta^{\text{OLS}} .

$|\beta|$ is not differentiable at $0$, so we use the subgradient: the set
of slopes of lines lying below the function. For $|\beta|$ it is
Setting $0\in\partial g$:

items: $\beta>0$: $2(\beta-b)+\lambda=0 \Rightarrow \beta=b-\lambda/2$, valid when $b>\lambda/2$.
$\beta<0$: $\beta=b+\lambda/2$, valid when $b<-\lambda/2$.
$\beta=0$: requires $|2b|\le\lambda$, i.e. $|b|\le\lambda/2$.

blocks.t:
The third case is the crucial one: whenever $|b|\le\lambda/2$, zero is a
valid solution — because at $\beta=0$ the penalty has a whole interval
of subgradients, and the loss gradient only has to fall somewhere inside it. That
interval is what a squared penalty lacks: $\frac{d}{d\beta}\beta^2=2\beta=0$ at
the origin, a single point that provides no such slack.
The geometry

blocks.cap:
The constrained view of both penalties on identical data. The $L_1$
 ball is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes, so the elliptical
 contours very often first touch a corner — giving a solution with a
 coefficient exactly zero. The $L_2$ ball is round, so the touch point is
 generically off-axis.

blocks.t: The one-line version

$\|\beta\|_1\le t$ is a diamond with corners on the axes.
$\|\beta\|_2\le t$ is a circle with no corners. A corner is exactly a
point where some coordinate is zero, and convex contours meet corners
disproportionately often. In $p$ dimensions the $L_1$ ball has $2p$ vertices and
many lower-dimensional edges and faces, all of which set some coefficients to
zero — so sparsity becomes more likely, not less, as $p$ grows.
Feature Selection as a By-Product
Embedded selection

Lasso belongs to the embedded family of feature-selection methods
(Topic 12): selection happens inside training rather than as a separate
filter or wrapper step. That makes it cheap — one fit gives you both a model and
a feature subset — and it means the selection is made with respect to the actual
predictive objective rather than a proxy statistic.
Why There Is No Closed Form
The absolute value is not differentiable

Ridge's derivation ends with a linear system because
$\frac{d}{d\beta}\beta^2=2\beta$ everywhere. Lasso's $|\beta|$ has a kink at zero,
so you cannot set a single derivative to zero and solve.

The standard algorithm is coordinate descent: cycle through the
coefficients, and update each one in turn using the soft-thresholding formula
while holding the others fixed. Each update is exact and closed-form, and the
whole cycle converges quickly. This is what scikit-learn's Lasso does — it
is why the class exposes max_iter and tol, and why you occasionally
see a ConvergenceWarning that a Ridge fit would never produce.
Limitations
Three real weaknesses

items:
With correlated features, Lasso picks one arbitrarily. Given two
 nearly identical predictors, it keeps one and zeroes the other, and which
 one it keeps can flip with a small change in the data. Ridge instead
 splits the weight between them. This instability is the main motivation
 for Elastic Net (Topic 43).

At most $n$ features survive. When $p>n$, Lasso can select at
 most $n$ non-zero coefficients — a hard structural limit, awkward in
 genomics and text where $p\gg n$.

The selection is not always the true model. Lasso's consistency
 requires an "irrepresentable condition" on the correlation structure
 that real data frequently violates. Treat the selected set as a useful
 subset, not as a discovery of the true predictors.

blocks.t: $\lambda$ and its effect, from the notes

Higher lambda $\to$ underfit (more coefficients driven to zero, until
only the intercept remains). Lower lambda $\to$ overfitting
($\lambda=0$ recovers OLS exactly). As always, tune it by cross-validation, and
standardise first — the penalty is unit-dependent for the same reason as Ridge.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import (Lasso, LassoCV, Ridge, LinearRegression,
                                  ElasticNet, lars_path)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p = 150, 20
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p))
true_w = np.zeros(p); true_w[:4] = [3., -2., 1.5, 2.]      # only 4 real features
y = X @ true_w + rng.normal(0, 1., n)

# =====================================================================
# 1. SHRINKS SOME WEIGHTS TO EXACTLY ZERO
# =====================================================================
las = Lasso(alpha=0.3).fit(X, y)
rid = Ridge(alpha=0.3).fit(X, y)
print("Lasso coefficients:", las.coef_.round(3))
print("Ridge coefficients:", rid.coef_.round(3))
print(f"\nexact zeros -- Lasso: {int((las.coef_ == 0).sum())} of {p}")
print(f"exact zeros -- Ridge: {int((rid.coef_ == 0).sum())} of {p}")
print("Lasso kept features:", np.flatnonzero(las.coef_),
      " (the true ones are 0,1,2,3)")

# =====================================================================
# 2. SOFT-THRESHOLDING -- the operator that produces the zeros
# =====================================================================
def soft_threshold(b, lam):
    """sign(b) * max(|b| - lam/2, 0)   -- SUBTRACT then clip."""
    return np.sign(b) * np.maximum(np.abs(b) - lam/2, 0.0)

def ridge_shrink(b, lam):
    """b / (1 + lam)   -- DIVIDE, so it can never reach zero."""
    return b / (1 + lam)

print(f"\n{'OLS beta':>10s} {'Lasso':>10s} {'Ridge':>10s}   (lambda = 1.0)")
for b in [3.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.4, 0.2, 0.0, -0.3, -2.0]:
    print(f"{b:10.2f} {soft_threshold(b, 1.0):10.3f} {ridge_shrink(b, 1.0):10.3f}")
# Everything with |beta| <= 0.5 becomes EXACTLY 0 under Lasso.
# Nothing ever becomes exactly 0 under Ridge.

# VERIFY on orthonormal data, where the closed forms are exact:
Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(0, 1, (400, 6)))
yq = Q @ np.array([2.5, -1.2, 0.35, 0.15, -0.05, 1.8]) + rng.normal(0, .05, 400)
ols_q = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit(Q, yq).coef_
lam = 0.6
las_q = Lasso(alpha=lam/2/len(yq)*len(yq)/2, fit_intercept=False,
              max_iter=100000).fit(Q, yq).coef_       # sklearn scales by n
print("\nOLS            :", ols_q.round(4))
print("soft-threshold :", soft_threshold(ols_q, lam).round(4))
print("Ridge formula  :", ridge_shrink(ols_q, lam).round(4))

# =====================================================================
# 3. HIGHER LAMBDA -> UNDERFIT;  LOWER LAMBDA -> OVERFIT
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'lambda':>10s} {'non-zero':>10s} {'train R2':>10s} {'cv R2':>9s}")
for a in [0.0001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 3.0, 10.0]:
    m = Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=50000).fit(X, y)
    cv = cross_val_score(Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=50000), X, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{a:10.4f} {int((m.coef_ != 0).sum()):10d} {m.score(X, y):10.4f} {cv:9.4f}")
# alpha -> 0 keeps every feature and overfits (cv R2 falls).
# alpha large kills every feature -> the model predicts the mean, R2 -> 0.

print("\nat alpha=10 the model is just the intercept:",
      Lasso(alpha=10).fit(X, y).coef_.round(6))

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE REGULARISATION PATH -- watch features drop out one by one
# =====================================================================
alphas = np.logspace(-3, 0.8, 40)
print(f"\n{'alpha':>9s}  surviving features")
for a in alphas[::6]:
    c = Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=50000).fit(X, y).coef_
    print(f"{a:9.4f}  {np.flatnonzero(c)}")
# Irrelevant features leave first; the four real ones survive longest.

# LARS computes the ENTIRE path exactly, at the cost of one OLS fit:
_, _, coefs = lars_path(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), y, method="lasso")
print(f"\nLARS path has {coefs.shape[1]} breakpoints "
      f"(each is a feature entering or leaving)")

# =====================================================================
# 5. NO CLOSED FORM -- coordinate descent, implemented
# =====================================================================
def lasso_coordinate_descent(X, y, lam, n_iter=1000, tol=1e-8):
    """Cycle through coefficients, soft-thresholding each in turn."""
    X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
    n, p = X.shape
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    y = y - y.mean()
    for _ in range(n_iter):
        beta_old = beta.copy()
        for j in range(p):
            # residual with feature j removed
            r_j = y - X @ beta + X[:, j] * beta[j]
            rho = X[:, j] @ r_j / n
            z   = (X[:, j] ** 2).sum() / n
            beta[j] = np.sign(rho) * max(abs(rho) - lam, 0) / z   # soft threshold
        if np.abs(beta - beta_old).max() < tol:
            break
    return beta

b_cd = lasso_coordinate_descent(X, y, lam=0.3)
b_sk = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Lasso(alpha=0.3, max_iter=50000)).fit(X, y)[-1].coef_
print(f"\ncoordinate descent vs sklearn: max diff {np.abs(b_cd - b_sk).max():.5f}")
print(f"same features selected: "
      f"{set(np.flatnonzero(b_cd)) == set(np.flatnonzero(b_sk))}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. LIMITATION 1 -- with correlated features it picks ARBITRARILY
# =====================================================================
Xc = X.copy()
Xc[:, 5] = Xc[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, .01, n)        # a near-duplicate of feature 0
yc = Xc @ true_w + rng.normal(0, 1., n)

print("\nfeature 0 and feature 5 are nearly identical:")
for seed in range(5):
    idx = np.random.default_rng(seed).choice(n, n, replace=True)   # bootstrap
    c = Lasso(alpha=0.2, max_iter=50000).fit(Xc[idx], yc[idx]).coef_
    print(f"  sample {seed}: beta_0 {c[0]:7.3f}  beta_5 {c[5]:7.3f}")
# It keeps one and zeroes the other, and WHICH one flips between samples.

print("\nRidge splits the weight instead:")
c = Ridge(alpha=0.2).fit(Xc, yc).coef_
print(f"  beta_0 {c[0]:.3f}  beta_5 {c[5]:.3f}  (sum {c[0]+c[5]:.3f})")

print("\nElastic Net keeps BOTH (Topic 43):")
c = ElasticNet(alpha=0.2, l1_ratio=0.5, max_iter=50000).fit(Xc, yc).coef_
print(f"  beta_0 {c[0]:.3f}  beta_5 {c[5]:.3f}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. LIMITATION 2 -- at most n features can be selected when p > n
# =====================================================================
n2, p2 = 50, 500
X2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (n2, p2))
w2 = np.zeros(p2); w2[:80] = rng.normal(0, 2, 80)   # 80 TRUE features
y2 = X2 @ w2 + rng.normal(0, 1, n2)

for a in [0.05, 0.01, 0.001]:
    k = int((Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=50000).fit(X2, y2).coef_ != 0).sum())
    print(f"\nalpha={a}: selected {k} features (n={n2}, true non-zero = 80)")
# It can never exceed n, no matter how small alpha gets.

# =====================================================================
# 8. TUNING, AND STANDARDISATION
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

lcv = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    LassoCV(alphas=np.logspace(-4, 1, 80), cv=5,
                            max_iter=50000, random_state=0)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nLassoCV chose alpha = {lcv[-1].alpha_:.5f}")
print(f"features kept: {int((lcv[-1].coef_ != 0).sum())} of {p}")
print(f"test R2 -- Lasso {lcv.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}   "
      f"Ridge {make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=1)).fit(X_tr,y_tr).score(X_te,y_te):.4f}   "
      f"OLS {LinearRegression().fit(X_tr,y_tr).score(X_te,y_te):.4f}")
# With 16 of 20 features irrelevant, Lasso should win clearly.

# Scaling matters exactly as it does for Ridge:
Xu = X.copy(); Xu[:, 0] *= 1000
print("\nunscaled -- feature 0 kept?",
      Lasso(alpha=0.3).fit(Xu, y).coef_[0] != 0,
      " scaled -- kept?",
      make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Lasso(alpha=0.3)).fit(Xu, y)[-1].coef_[0] != 0)
Worked Examples
Soft-thresholding: how Lasso sets coefficients to exactly zero
One-feature Lasso with objective $\tfrac12 (z - w)^2 + \lambda |w|$, where $z$ is the unpenalised least-squares answer. Its solution is the soft-threshold operator
\hat w = S(z,\lambda) = \operatorname{sign}(z) \max(|z|-\lambda, 0)
With $\lambda = 1$:

head: $z$
$|z| - \lambda$
Lasso $\hat w$
Ridge $z/(1+\lambda)$
note
rows: both shrink; Lasso by a fixed amount

blocks.t: The contrast. Lasso subtracts a constant $\lambda$ from $|z|$ and clips at zero, so a small enough signal is removed completely. Ridge multiplies by $1/(1+\lambda)$, which never reaches zero. This is why Lasso performs feature selection and Ridge does not.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Lasso reduces overfitting by shrinking weights, and some weights
 become exactly zero. Thus effectively it does feature selection.

Loss $=$ Loss $+$ Penalty, with an absolute penalty:
 $L=\text{Loss}+\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|$, $\lambda\ge0$.
Higher lambda $\to$ underfit. Lower lambda $\to$ overfitting.

As $\lambda$ increases the corresponding coefficients become
 zero. For Ridge they get near 0; for Lasso exactly 0.

The notes' intuition is literally true: in the orthonormal case Ridge
 gives $\hat\beta/(1+\lambda)$ — $\lambda$ in the denominator —
 while Lasso gives
 $\operatorname{sign}(\hat\beta)(|\hat\beta|-\lambda/2)_+$ — $\lambda$
 subtracted. Division never reaches zero; subtraction with
 clipping does.

The reason is the subgradient: $|\beta|$ has an entire interval
 $[-1,1]$ of subgradients at zero, giving the optimiser slack that $\beta^2$
 (a single point) does not provide.

Geometrically, the $L_1$ ball is a diamond with corners on the
 axes; the $L_2$ ball is a circle with none.

No closed form — solved by coordinate descent using
 soft-thresholding.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked

Q. Why does Lasso produce exactly zero coefficients but Ridge does
not?

In the orthonormal case Ridge divides each coefficient by $1+\lambda$, and
division by a positive number never gives zero. Lasso subtracts
$\lambda/2$ and clips at zero, so any coefficient smaller than $\lambda/2$
becomes exactly zero. Geometrically, the $L_1$ constraint region is a diamond with
corners on the axes; the $L_2$ region is a smooth circle.
Q. Explain the subgradient argument.

$|\beta|$ is not differentiable at zero; its subgradient there is the whole
interval $[-1,1]$. Zero is optimal whenever the loss gradient falls anywhere
inside that interval, which happens for a whole range of data. $\beta^2$ has
derivative $2\beta$, a single value of zero at the origin, providing no such
slack.
Q. When would you choose Lasso over Ridge?

When you believe many features are irrelevant and you want automatic selection, or
when you need a sparse, deployable model. Choose Ridge when all features are
believed relevant, or when the features are highly correlated and you want stable
coefficients rather than an arbitrary pick.
Q. Why is there no closed-form solution for Lasso?

Because the absolute value is not differentiable at zero, so you cannot set a
single derivative to zero and solve a linear system. Coordinate descent solves it
by cycling through coefficients, each update being an exact soft-threshold.
Q. Two features are near-duplicates. What does Lasso do?

It keeps one and zeroes the other, essentially arbitrarily — and which one it
keeps can flip with a small change in the data. Ridge splits the weight between
them. Elastic Net (Topic 43) combines both penalties precisely to fix this
instability.
Q. You have 500 features and 50 rows. What is Lasso's limit?

It can select at most 50 non-zero coefficients — a structural limit of the
optimisation, regardless of how small $\lambda$ is. If you believe more than $n$
features are genuinely predictive, use Elastic Net.
Q. Can you interpret the selected features as "the important ones"?

With caution. Lasso's selection consistency requires conditions on the
correlation structure that real data often violates, and with correlated
predictors the choice is partly arbitrary. Treat the selection as a useful
subset, and confirm importance by other means before making claims.
